newsitem.title: CANADA: Quebec says Hydro-Quebec can study river diversion.
newsitem.headline: Quebec says Hydro-Quebec can study river diversion.

text.p: The Quebec government said on Wednesday it authorized Hydro-Quebec to study the diversion of four rivers in northern Quebec to increase output at three of its generating stations.

"The cabinet authorizes Hydro-Quebec to begin preliminary work on the diversion of the Portneuf, Sault-aux-Cochons, Manouane and Boucher rivers," Natural Resources minister Guy Chevrette said in a statement.
The government-owned utility will be able to start scientific and environmental impact studies on the project. If approved, the project could cost C$100 million and create 1,000 jobs.

The announcement came after a story on Wednesday in the Montreal daily newspaper Le Devoir, which said Hydro-Quebec Chief Executive Andre Caille had filed the river diversion request with the provincial government on March 14.
Hydro-Quebec asked permission to divert rivers in the North Shore and Lac-Saint-Jean region to help feed its Bersimis 1 and 2 and Outardes 3 generating stations.

The government said the diversion of the Portneuf, Sault-aux-Cochons and Maenouane rivers would increase the water flow in the Pipmuacan reservoir, resulting in a net increase of 1 terrawatt hour for the Bersimis 1 and 2 generating stations.
The diversion of the Boucher River would increase output at the Outardes 3 generating facility by 0.2 TWh.
Hydro-Quebec spokesman Guy Litalien disputed a newspaper report that the utility's reservoirs were short of water.
"We are not lacking water. We are doing this project because we think it will be profitable and because we could export the energy to the United States," Litalien told Reuters.
Quebec Environment Minister David Cliche told reporters the project would not go ahead without public hearings.
Hydro-Quebec generates, distributes and markets most of the electricity produced in Quebec, and exports some output to clients in the northeastern United States.
